etymology: From Old French cuivre, of Germanic origin.
biblical_def: The case for arrows used by warriors and hunters; in Psalm 127, a metaphor for many children — the man whose quiver is full is blessed.
webster_summary: Arrow-case; metaphor for children as blessing.
webster_full: A case for carrying arrows; in Psalm 127:5 used as the great metaphor for children — happy is the man whose quiver is full of them; in Isaiah 49:2 the LORD makes His Servant 'a polished shaft' and hides Him in His quiver.
scriptures: Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them: they shall not be ashamed, but they shall speak with the enemies in the gate.
And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft, and in his quiver hath he hid me.
He hath caused the arrows of his quiver to enter into my reins.
corruption_summary: Cultural code-language for opposition to family planning, missing the original blessing-language Scripture intends.
corruption_paragraphs: The metaphor in Psalm 127 is blessing, not weapon. Children are arrows the godly man sends into the future. The verse calls children gift; subcultures have made it shorthand for movements. Recover the original delight.
usage: Children are arrows; the quiver is blessing.
The Servant is hidden in the quiver of God.

etymology: From Old English cwencan "to extinguish."
biblical_def: To extinguish; especially Paul's command not to quench the Spirit (1 Thess 5:19); also the unquenchable fire of judgment (Mark 9:43-48) and the fiery darts faith quenches (Eph 6:16).
webster_summary: To extinguish; what we do or fail to do with the Spirit.
webster_full: To put out, extinguish, suppress; Paul commands not to quench the Spirit (1 Thess 5:19); contrasted with Mark's 'fire that shall never be quenched' of judgment; and Ephesians' shield of faith that quenches the fiery darts of the wicked one.
scriptures: Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked.
Where the worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.
corruption_summary: Reduced to physical extinguishing; missing the spiritual sense of resisting the Spirit's prompting.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's three-word command — 'quench not the Spirit' — has weight. The Spirit can be grieved; He can be quenched. Persistent resistance, indifference, and disobedience put out His fire in our hearts. Be careful what you damp.
usage: Quench not the Spirit.
Faith quenches the fiery darts.

etymology: Latin quaternio — "a group of four," Roman military squad.
biblical_def: A Roman military squad of four soldiers; Herod assigned four quaternions (sixteen total) to guard imprisoned Peter (Acts 12:4) — from whom an angel led him out.
webster_summary: A Roman squad of four; Peter's prison guard.
webster_full: A Roman military squad of four soldiers; Herod assigned four such quaternions (sixteen soldiers total, rotating in three-hour watches) to guard the imprisoned apostle Peter — and an angel of the Lord walked him out anyway.
scriptures: And when he had apprehended him, he put him in prison, and delivered him to four quaternions of soldiers to keep him; intending after Easter to bring him forth to the people.
And the same night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains... behold, the angel of the Lord came upon him.
Now I know of a surety, that the Lord hath sent his angel, and hath delivered me out of the hand of Herod.
corruption_summary: Forgotten as obscure detail, missing the deliberate Lukan emphasis on the impossibility of human security against God's purposes.
corruption_paragraphs: Sixteen soldiers in three-hour rotations, two chained directly to Peter, sealed in inner prison — and an angel walks him through. Luke records the security detail to make the point: when God sends His angel, no human guard holds. Read Acts 12 with the quaternion-detail in mind.
usage: Four quaternions could not hold Peter.
Read Acts 12 with security-detail in mind.

etymology: From Latin quinta essentia — "fifth essence," the ancient philosophical 'fifth element' beyond earth, water, fire, air.
biblical_def: Not a biblical word, but a useful concept: the purest distilled essence of something. Christ is the quintessence of God's glory (Heb 1:3) — the brightness of His glory, the express image of His person.
webster_summary: Purest distilled essence of something.
webster_full: The purest, most concentrated essence; not biblical vocabulary but useful for what Hebrews 1:3 says of Christ — He is the brightness of God's glory and the express image of His person, the quintessential revelation of who God is.
scriptures: Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power.
He that hath seen me hath seen the Father.
Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.
corruption_summary: Used loosely in modern English, severed from its precise meaning of distilled-essence.
corruption_paragraphs: When we say Christ is the quintessence of God's glory, we mean Hebrews 1:3 precisely: He is not a sample of God but the purest distilled revelation of who God is. To see Christ is to see the Father, undiluted, unshadowed, perfect.
usage: Christ is the quintessence of God's revelation.
Hebrews 1:3 is the warrant.

etymology: From Old English geldan "to repay, render."
biblical_def: Surrendered, presented, handed-over; Paul's central language for offering oneself to God (Rom 6:13, 16, 19; 12:1) — yielded members and yielded body.
webster_summary: Surrendered, handed over; Paul's offering-language.
webster_full: Surrendered, presented, given over for use; Paul's central image for the disciple's relationship to God — the body and its members yielded as instruments of righteousness rather than of unrighteousness; the climactic 'present your bodies a living sacrifice' of Romans 12:1.
scriptures: Neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin: but yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead.
Even so now yield your members servants to righteousness unto holiness.
I beseech you therefore, brethren... that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice.
corruption_summary: Modernized translations have dropped the term, weakening Paul's urgent call to surrender.
corruption_paragraphs: The yielded life is the disciple's life — body, members, will all handed over to the new Master. Romans 6 develops the language extensively. Yieldedness is not passivity; it is active offering. Yield to God, not to sin.
usage: Yield your members to righteousness.
Yieldedness is active surrender.

etymology: From Old English giernan "to long for."
biblical_def: To long deeply, ache, be moved with strong desire; Joseph 'yearned upon' his brothers (Gen 43:30); Paul yearns for the Philippians 'in the bowels of Christ' (Phil 1:8); the deer yearns for the streams (Ps 42:1).
webster_summary: To long deeply with strong moving desire.
webster_full: To long deeply, ache with desire, be moved in the inward parts; used of Joseph's emotion before his brothers, Paul's yearning for distant churches, and the soul's longing for God in the Psalms.
scriptures: And Joseph made haste; for his bowels did yearn upon his brother: and he sought where to weep.
For God is my record, how greatly I long after you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ.
As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.
corruption_summary: Replaced in modern English by weaker words; the visceral 'bowels of compassion' language is largely lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrew and Greek both locate strong emotion in the bowels — kidneys, gut, viscera. Paul yearns 'in the bowels of Christ,' meaning with the same gut-level affection Christ felt for His own. Recover yearning as a spiritual category.
usage: Yearn for God; yearn for His people.
Recover bowels-of-Christ affection.

etymology: Greek neōterikai epithymiai — desires of youth.
biblical_def: The cluster of immature, ungoverned desires Paul charges Timothy to flee — sexual sin, disputatiousness, attention-craving, status-seeking (2 Tim 2:22).
webster_summary: Cluster of immature ungoverned desires.
webster_full: The plural Greek term Paul uses (neōterikai epithymiai) for the cluster of youth-typical desires — not sexual lust alone but also disputatiousness, attention-craving, status-seeking — that the young Timothy is to flee, pursuing instead righteousness, faith, love, and peace with pure-hearted believers.
scriptures: Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.
Young men likewise exhort to be sober minded.
corruption_summary: Read narrowly as sexual sin; missing Paul's broader cluster including pride and contentiousness.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's plural — 'youthful lusts' — is wider than sex. It includes the young man's tendency to argue, to crave attention, to chase status. The young pastor must flee them all and pursue the four-fold positive: righteousness, faith, love, peace. Read 2 Timothy 2:22 widely.
usage: Flee youthful lusts; pursue four-fold righteousness.
The cluster is wider than sex.

etymology: From Old English geara "long ago."
biblical_def: An archaic adverb meaning 'long ago, in olden times'; appears in the KJV as 'of old' or 'in days of yore'; Hebrew olam, qedem.
webster_summary: Long ago; in olden times.
webster_full: Archaic English adverb meaning 'long ago' or 'in olden times'; surfaces in older Bible translations and hymns; Hebrew counterparts olam (eternity, age) and qedem (former, ancient) carry similar weight in passages on God's eternal purposes.
scriptures: Remember the days of old, consider the years of many generations: ask thy father, and he will shew thee.
I have considered the days of old, the years of ancient times.
But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah... out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.
corruption_summary: Lost from common speech; with it the appreciation for biblical 'days of old' has dimmed.
corruption_paragraphs: The Bible repeatedly calls us to remember the days of yore — God's old works as basis for present trust. Modern presentism cuts the cord. Recover the long memory; sing the old hymns; trust the old promises.
usage: Remember the days of yore.
God's old works ground present trust.

etymology: Compound of yoke and fellow; KJV translation of Greek syzygos — "yoked-together one."
biblical_def: A fellow-laborer joined under the same yoke of ministry; Paul's affectionate term in Philippians 4:3 for an unnamed (or perhaps proper-named) gospel co-worker.
webster_summary: Fellow-laborer joined under the same yoke.
webster_full: A fellow-laborer in the gospel joined under the same yoke; Paul's affectionate term in Philippians 4:3 for an unnamed (or perhaps proper-named) gospel co-worker, asked to help Euodia and Syntyche reconcile.
scriptures: And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel.
Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart... For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
corruption_summary: Lost vocabulary; with it has gone the recognition of partnered ministry as a category.
corruption_paragraphs: Yoked partners pull together. Paul's ministry was full of yoke-fellows — Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, Titus, Epaphras, the unnamed in Philippians 4. Solo ministry violates the picture. Find your yoke-fellows.
usage: Find your yoke-fellow in ministry.
Solo ministry breaks the picture.

etymology: Hebrew Tsofar (צוֹפַר) — "sparrow" or "chirper."
biblical_def: The third of Job's three friends, a Naamathite; the harshest accuser, insisting Job's suffering proves hidden sin (Job 11; 20); rebuked at the end with the others.
webster_summary: Job's third friend; the harshest accuser.
webster_full: The third of Job's three friends, a Naamathite; characteristically the most direct and harshest accuser, charging Job to repent of supposed hidden sin and warning of the doom of the wicked; rebuked by God at the end with Eliphaz and Bildad.
scriptures: But oh that God would speak... and that he would shew thee the secrets of wisdom... Know therefore that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth.
That the triumphing of the wicked is short, and the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment.
My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath.
corruption_summary: Treated only as a backdrop figure; missing how Zophar epitomizes the well-meaning hard counselor whose theology is too small.
corruption_paragraphs: Zophar represents the dangerous counselor whose theology has no place for innocent suffering. He tells Job he is being treated less harshly than he deserves. He is rebuked. Beware Zophar-counsel; it presses sufferers further into despair.
usage: Beware Zophar-counsel toward sufferers.
His theology was too small for Job's reality.

etymology: Hebrew Tsidqiyahu (צִדְקִיָּהוּ) — "YHWH is my righteousness."
biblical_def: The last king of Judah (~597-586 BC), placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar; rebelled against Babylon, was defeated, and saw his sons killed before being blinded and led captive (2 Kings 24-25; Jer 39).
webster_summary: Judah's last king before the exile.
webster_full: The last king of Judah, son of Josiah, placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar at the second deportation; rebelled against Babylon, was captured at Jericho when Jerusalem fell, watched his sons killed before his eyes were put out, and was led in chains to Babylon — a tragic close to David's monarchy.
scriptures: So they took the king, and brought him up to the king of Babylon to Riblah; and they gave judgment upon him. And they slew the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and put out the eyes of Zedekiah.
Behold, he is in your hand: for the king is not he that can do any thing against you.
I will bring him to Babylon to the land of the Chaldeans; yet shall he not see it, though he shall die there.
corruption_summary: Forgotten as one of many bad kings; missing how thoroughly his life dramatizes the cost of refusing prophetic word.
corruption_paragraphs: Zedekiah's name means 'YHWH is my righteousness' but his life was the opposite. Jeremiah pleaded with him to surrender; he refused; the city fell; his sons died; he was blinded. The last sight he saw was his sons killed. Cost of rejecting the prophet.
usage: Heed the prophet earlier than Zedekiah did.
His name promised what his life refused.

etymology: Old English negation of defiled.
biblical_def: Pure, unstained, free from ceremonial or moral pollution; applied to Christ (Heb 7:26), to the inheritance reserved for believers (1 Pet 1:4), to true religion (James 1:27), and to the marriage bed (Heb 13:4).
webster_summary: Pure, unstained; applied to Christ, the inheritance, and the bed.
webster_full: Pure, unstained, free from ceremonial or moral pollution; an attribute of Christ Himself, of the heavenly inheritance reserved for the saints, of pure religion before the Father, and of the bed within marriage.
scriptures: For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens.
To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you.
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: Reduced to ritual purity language; Scripture uses it of moral and eschatological reality.
corruption_paragraphs: Undefiled in Hebrews 7 says something about Christ; in 1 Peter 1, about your inheritance; in James 1, about religion; in Hebrews 13, about marriage. The purity is real, not ceremonial. The Christ who is undefiled keeps undefiled what He claims.
usage: Christ is undefiled; so is your inheritance.
Marriage bed and pure religion both.

etymology: English compound; Greek apistos — without faith.
biblical_def: One who has not believed the gospel and remains in unbelief; a category Paul uses for clear distinction in marriage, partnership, and judgment matters (1 Cor 7:14; 2 Cor 6:14; 1 Cor 14:22-25).
webster_summary: One who has not believed the gospel.
webster_full: One who has not believed the gospel and remains in unbelief; Paul's distinct category from the 'brother' for purposes of marriage (1 Cor 7), partnership (2 Cor 6), and worship-context (1 Cor 14); a real category, not stigma.
scriptures: Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness?
For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife... if the unbelieving depart, let him depart.
But brother goeth to law with brother, and that before the unbelievers.
corruption_summary: Avoided as too judgmental; Paul uses it directly without apology to make practical distinctions.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul does not pejoratively call people unbelievers; he distinguishes categories so believers can navigate marriage, partnership, and worship rightly. The category is not insult — it is reality. Pretending all are believers leads to bad counsel and confused obedience.
usage: Use the category honestly for practical decisions.
Distinct from insult; just descriptive.

etymology: Old English negation of spotted.
biblical_def: Free from the world's stains; the second half of pure religion in James 1:27 — to visit orphans and widows AND to keep oneself unspotted from the world.
webster_summary: Free from world-stains.
webster_full: Free from the world's contaminating stains; the second half of pure religion in James 1:27 — visit orphans and widows AND keep oneself unspotted from the world; an active discipline of moral and spiritual cleanness in the midst of a corrupting culture.
scriptures: Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
That thou keep this commandment without spot, unrebukeable, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.
corruption_summary: Often dropped from James 1:27 sermons; contemporary ethics emphasizes the visit-the-widow without the unspotted-from-world.
corruption_paragraphs: James 1:27 has two halves: visit and keep unspotted. Cultural Christianity loves the first; cringes at the second. Pure religion requires both. Compassion AND moral separation. Embrace one without the other and the religion is no longer pure.
usage: Visit AND keep unspotted.
Both halves are pure religion.

etymology: Old English negation of stable.
biblical_def: Wavering, unsteady, double-minded; the marker of those who twist Scripture to their own destruction (2 Pet 3:16) and the double-minded who get nothing in prayer (James 1:8).
webster_summary: Wavering; double-minded; unsettled.
webster_full: The unsteady soul: double-minded in James 1:8 (gets nothing from prayer), unsteady in 2 Peter 2:14 and 3:16 (twisting Scripture and following error), wavering between two opinions; opposite of the established believer rooted and grounded in love.
scriptures: A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.
In which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.
Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel.
corruption_summary: Often pathologized as 'mental health'; while sometimes that, Scripture's primary use is moral-spiritual unsteadiness.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture's unstable man is not first medical — he is moral. He is double-minded, divided in loyalty, wavering between God and world. The cure is single-mindedness, rooted faith, and the steady habits Paul calls 'rooted and grounded.' Pursue stability.
usage: Pursue stability through single-mindedness.
Double-minded gets nothing from prayer.

etymology: Old English; to hold up, sustain.
biblical_def: To hold up, sustain, support; God's promise to uphold His people by His righteous right hand (Isa 41:10), His Servant by His Spirit (Isa 42:1), and the universe by the word of His power (Heb 1:3).
webster_summary: To hold up, sustain; God's action toward His people.
webster_full: To hold up, sustain, support; God's verb regarding His people ('I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness'), His chosen Servant ('whom I uphold'), and creation itself ('upholding all things by the word of his power').
scriptures: Fear thou not; for I am with thee... I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth.
And upholding all things by the word of his power.
corruption_summary: Reduced to legal-formal language ('upholds the constitution'), missing the personal-supportive sense in Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 41:10 is one of Scripture's great upholding verses. The God who upholds the universe by the word of His power upholds His people by His righteous right hand. Same God; same upholding power. Lean on it.
usage: I will uphold thee — the great promise.
He upholds all things by His word.

etymology: From Latin vagari "to wander."
biblical_def: A wanderer without settled home; God's curse on Cain (Gen 4:12); a category of unsettled exorcists in Acts 19:13. Negative connotation in Scripture.
webster_summary: Wanderer without settled home; Cain's curse.
webster_full: A wanderer without settled home or purpose; the specific curse on Cain after the murder of Abel ('a fugitive and vagabond shalt thou be'); also the description of certain itinerant Jewish exorcists in Acts 19:13. A condition of judgment, not blessing.
scriptures: When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.
Behold, thou hast driven me out this day from the face of the earth; and from thy face shall I be hid; and I shall be a fugitive and a vagabond in the earth.
Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus.
corruption_summary: Romanticized in modern culture as the free wanderer; Scripture treats it as a state of judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Vagabond romanticism inverts the biblical picture. Cain's wandering was curse, not freedom. Settled rootedness — in family, in church, in covenant land — is biblical blessing. Wandering disconnected from home is judgment unfulfilled, not autonomy fulfilled.
usage: Vagabondage is curse, not freedom.
Settle in covenant; root in church.

etymology: From Old French vaillant "strong, brave."
biblical_def: Brave, courageous, mighty in battle; a frequent KJV term for warriors (1 Sam 14:52), David's mighty men (2 Sam 23), and the faithful in Hebrews 11:34 who 'waxed valiant in fight.'
webster_summary: Brave, courageous, mighty in battle.
webster_full: Brave, courageous, mighty in battle; a frequent KJV term for warriors, especially David's mighty men, the men of valor enrolled by Saul, and the faithful of Hebrews 11 who 'out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.'
scriptures: These be the names of the mighty men whom David had: The Tachmonite that sat in the seat, chief among the captains.
Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight.
And there was sore war against the Philistines all the days of Saul: and when Saul saw any strong man, or any valiant man, he took him unto him.
corruption_summary: Lost from common speech; with it the category of biblical warrior-courage has dimmed.
corruption_paragraphs: Christianity needs the valiant. Hebrews 11 lists faithful who waxed valiant in fight. Faith does not make us passive; sometimes it requires the warrior's posture. Pray for valiant brothers and sisters in our generation.
usage: Be valiant for the truth.
Pray for valiant brothers.

etymology: From Latin vehemens — "impetuous, ardent."
biblical_def: Strong, fervent, forceful; used of Jonah's east wind (Jonah 4:8), the rushing mighty wind at Pentecost (Acts 2:2), and the godly sorrow that produced 'vehement desire' to make right (2 Cor 7:11).
webster_summary: Strong, forceful, fervent.
webster_full: Strong, forceful, fervent in feeling or action; in Scripture used of natural forces (the wind God prepared for Jonah, the rushing mighty wind at Pentecost) and of moral-spiritual urgency (the vehement desire of repentant Corinthians to set things right).
scriptures: And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty (vehement) wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting.
And it came to pass, when the sun did arise, that God prepared a vehement east wind.
What carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge!
corruption_summary: Faded from common speech; with it the precise category of holy intensity has weakened.
corruption_paragraphs: Pentecost was vehement. Repentance can be vehement. The east wind God sends to teach Jonah was vehement. Christianity is not always quiet; sometimes it is rushing-mighty. Make room for vehement seasons of the Spirit.
usage: Make room for vehement Spirit-work.
Repentance can be vehement.

etymology: From Latin vexare "to harass."
biblical_def: Severe distress of spirit, harassment, agitation; Ecclesiastes' refrain 'all is vanity and vexation of spirit' (Eccl 1:14, 17; 2:11); also Lot was 'vexed' by the wicked deeds of Sodom (2 Pet 2:7-8).
webster_summary: Severe distress; harassment of spirit.
webster_full: Severe distress of spirit, harassment, agitation; Ecclesiastes' refrain ('all is vanity and vexation of spirit') for the futility of life under the sun apart from God; also Lot's daily vexation by the wicked deeds of Sodom.
scriptures: I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit.
Just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked... vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds.
The dimness shall not be such as was in her vexation.
corruption_summary: Reduced to mild annoyance; Scripture uses it for severe spiritual distress and the futility of godless life.
corruption_paragraphs: Vexation is more than annoyance. Lot was vexed daily — his righteous soul ached at Sodom's wickedness. Ecclesiastes finds vexation under the sun without God. Christians can expect to be vexed by the world's evil; that is conscience working, not malfunction.
roots_summary: Hebrew reut ruach — vexation of spirit.
usage: Be vexed at the world's evil — like Lot.
Vexation under the sun is the futility-cry.

etymology: From Old French verai + suffix; KJV translation of Greek amēn.
biblical_def: Truly; the KJV's standard rendering of Greek amēn introducing solemn declaration; in John uniquely doubled — "verily, verily" — for special emphasis (John 3:3; 5:24; 6:53).
webster_summary: Truly; KJV's translation of "Amen."
webster_full: The KJV adverb meaning 'truly,' translating Greek amēn; introduces solemn declarations especially of Christ; in John always doubled ('verily, verily') for heightened emphasis. The same word that closes our prayers opens Christ's most weighty statements.
scriptures: Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.
For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law.
corruption_summary: Modernized away in most translations, losing the link between Christ's solemn 'verily' and the Amen we say.
corruption_paragraphs: Jesus saying 'verily, verily' is Jesus saying 'amen, amen.' He puts His amen on the front of His statement; we put ours on the back of His promise. The same word frames the conversation. Recover the connection.
roots_summary: Greek amēn — truly, so be it.
usage: Verily, verily — Jesus' amen on the front.
Our amen on the back.

etymology: Hebrew qashar — to bind, knit; KJV image for deep covenantal friendship.
biblical_def: The deep covenantal bond described in 1 Samuel 18:1: 'the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul' — the model of biblical friendship.
webster_summary: The deep covenantal friendship-bond.
webster_full: The Hebrew image for the deepest covenantal friendship: souls knit together. The exemplar is Jonathan and David, whose covenant survived Jonathan's father's hatred, the wilderness flight, and Jonathan's death — extending in David's care for Mephibosheth.
scriptures: And it came to pass... that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul.
That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love.
corruption_summary: Sexualized by some modern readers, missing the historic Christian category of brotherly covenant friendship.
corruption_paragraphs: The David-Jonathan friendship is the Bible's great example of soul-knit brotherly love. Modern reading sometimes sexualizes it; the text and Hebrew context describe covenant brotherhood. Recover the category: men can love men's souls deeply, covenantally, and chastely.
usage: Pray for soul-knit friendships.
Jonathan and David are the model.

etymology: Middle English kinrede; family, relatives.
biblical_def: Family, relatives, kin; Abraham was called from his kindred (Gen 12:1); Boaz was kindred to Naomi (Ruth 2:1); the gospel goes to every kindred and tongue (Rev 5:9).
webster_summary: Family, relatives; the bond Abraham left and the gospel reaches.
webster_full: Family, relatives, kin; the natural bond of blood and household. Abraham was called from his kindred to a new land; Boaz's kindred made him kinsman-redeemer to Naomi; the redeemed in Revelation 5 come from every kindred, tongue, people, and nation.
scriptures: Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee.
And Naomi had a kinsman of her husband's, a mighty man of wealth, of the family of Elimelech; and his name was Boaz.
Thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation.
corruption_summary: Lost vocabulary; the natural categories of family and clan are diminishing in cultural reckoning.
corruption_paragraphs: Kindred matters in Scripture. The kinsman-redeemer required kindred. The Abrahamic call required leaving kindred. The eschaton brings all kindreds together at the throne. Family, clan, nation — biblical categories worth recovering.
usage: Kindred matters in Scripture's grammar.
All kindreds come to the throne.

etymology: Greek proverb of an ox kicking against the goad — futile resistance; spoken to Saul on the Damascus road.
biblical_def: Christ's word to Saul on the Damascus road (Acts 9:5; 26:14) — 'it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks' — comparing Saul's persecution to an ox's futile kicking against the goad.
webster_summary: Futile resistance to God's pursuing call.
webster_full: A Greek agricultural proverb: an ox kicking back against the goad only injures itself. Christ uses it on the Damascus road to describe Saul's persecution of the church — futile, painful resistance to the Lord's call already pursuing him.
scriptures: And the Lord said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.
I heard a voice speaking unto me, and saying in the Hebrew tongue, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.
But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Forgotten as obscure idiom, missing how vividly it pictures the futility of fighting God's call.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's words to Saul are pastoral as well as confrontational. The Lord had been pursuing Saul long before Damascus. The persecutor was the goaded ox kicking back. Many a long-resistant conversion has the same dynamic: the call has been there longer than we knew.
usage: Stop kicking against the goads.
The call has been there longer than you knew.

etymology: KJV translation of Hebrew goel ha-qarov — kinsman who is near.
biblical_def: The kinsman near enough in family relation to qualify as goel — kinsman-redeemer; in Ruth, the unnamed near kinsman who declines, allowing Boaz to redeem (Ruth 3:12; 4:1-8).
webster_summary: The kinsman qualified to redeem.
webster_full: The kinsman near enough in family to qualify under Mosaic law as redeemer of land or wife; in the Ruth narrative, the unnamed nearer kinsman who declines the role at the city gate, allowing Boaz (next in line) to redeem both the field and Ruth herself.
scriptures: And now it is true that I am thy near kinsman: howbeit there is a kinsman nearer than I.
And the kinsman said, I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I mar mine own inheritance: redeem thou my right to thyself; for I cannot redeem it.
If any of his kin come to redeem it, then shall he redeem that which his brother sold.
corruption_summary: Forgotten as legal detail, missing how the unnamed near kinsman's refusal makes Boaz's redemption possible — and types Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The unnamed near kinsman in Ruth 4 makes a quiet decision: he will not endanger his own inheritance to redeem Naomi's. Boaz steps in. The picture preaches: only One was both able and willing to redeem at full cost — Christ. The near kinsman declined; the great kinsman did not.
usage: The near kinsman declined; Boaz redeemed.
Christ alone is the great Kinsman-Redeemer.

etymology: From Old English geoguð "youth."
biblical_def: Pertaining to youth; in Scripture used both positively (Eccl 11:9, 'rejoice in thy youth') and warningly (2 Tim 2:22, 'flee youthful lusts'); the season of strength to be devoted to the Creator (Eccl 12:1).
webster_summary: Pertaining to the season of youth.
webster_full: Pertaining to the season of youth; in Scripture both a season of opportunity ('rejoice... in thy youth') and a season of risk ('flee youthful lusts'); above all the season Ecclesiastes commands to be devoted to the Creator before evil days come.
scriptures: Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not.
Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace.
For thou art my hope, O Lord GOD: thou art my trust from my youth.
corruption_summary: Idolized by youth-culture as the apex of life; Scripture treats it as the season of consecration before strength wanes.
corruption_paragraphs: Solomon's command in Ecclesiastes 12 frames youth as a stewardship: remember the Creator NOW. The age idolizes youth as life's apex; Scripture treats it as life's investment-window. Spend youthful strength on God before the evil days come.
roots_summary: Hebrew bachur — young man; neur — youth.
usage: Remember the Creator in your youth.
Spend strength on God; flee youthful lusts.
